title: What all share: the truths
hook: every school teaches the four truths and the eightfold path

segments.voice: Yesterday, many rafts, each one for crossing, not for carrying. Your line: many ways.

In Pali, in a monastery in Sri Lanka. In classical Chinese, in a temple in Taipei. In Tibetan, in a dharma hall in the Himalayas. In English, in a Zen center on a rainy evening. Different robes, bells and languages. Yet listen to what the teachers explain to new students, and the same short list keeps surfacing, the one the Buddha is said to have given in his very first teaching. After weeks on the differences, a new block begins: the schools side by side, ranked by no one, starting with what they hold in common.
screen: `PALI, CHINESE, TIBETAN, ENGLISH.` → `THE SAME SHORT LIST.` → `SIDE BY SIDE.`

segments.voice: Day four gave these truths with no jargon; now, how the schools hold them. First, where it starts. The discourse called Setting in Motion the Wheel of the Dhamma tells how the Buddha, after his awakening, went to the Deer Park near Benares and spoke to his old companions, a talk tradition counts as his first. Rhys Davids' translation has him name "the noble truth concerning suffering." Three more follow. Second, the four truths. There is suffering, dukkha: the ache, the unsatisfactoriness that runs through life. It has an arising: craving, the thirst that grasps. It has an ending: when craving is let go, the suffering stops. And there is a way to that ending. Third, the way: the noble eightfold path. Right view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness and concentration. Not eight steps to climb in order, teachers say, but eight strands of one rope. Fourth, how the schools hold them. Across the schools this course has visited, the four truths and the path turn up again and again. Theravada teaching keeps them close to the center, in the words of the Pali discourses. Mahayana teachers keep them too, and some read them through emptiness: the Heart Sutra, chanted in Mahayana temples, goes so far as to say there is no suffering, no arising, no ending and no path. Its teachers explain this not as throwing the truths away, but as holding even them without grasping. Some Tibetan teachers place the four truths at the beginning of the path, as the ground everything else stands on. Same truths, held in different hands.
screen: `THE DEER PARK, THE FIRST TEACHING.` · `SUFFERING, ARISING, ENDING, WAY.` · `EIGHT STRANDS OF ONE ROPE.` · `SAME TRUTHS, DIFFERENT HANDS.` · then, large: `SHARED BY ALL.`

segments.voice: Let the breath settle, then say the four truths slowly, one on each out-breath: there is suffering; suffering has an arising; suffering has an ending; there is a way. Let the eight strands of the path come to mind one by one, without trying to remember them perfectly. Notice which one feels closest today, speech perhaps, or effort, or mindfulness, and rest there.
What all share. The four noble truths and the eightfold path, taught across the Buddhist schools in their own languages and their own ways. Today's word.
Your line: shared by all. Four truths, eight strands, many languages. Day thirteen sixty, done.

screen: `DAY 1360 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHAT ALL SHARE: THE JEWELS.`

howItsDone: Teachers in the Buddhist schools teach the four noble truths and the eightfold path to beginners, and Buddhists chant or recite them, in Pali, Chinese, Tibetan, Japanese, English and other languages.

chat.says: Do Theravada and Mahayana Buddhists even believe the same basic things?
options: Yes, at the core: both teach the four truths and the eightfold path, in their own ways.
No. Mahayana Buddhists dropped the four truths, since the Heart Sutra says there are none.
No. Only Theravada teaches the eightfold path; Mahayana teaches devotion in its place.
chat.meaning: The four noble truths and the eightfold path turn up across the schools; Mahayana teachers keep them too, some reading them through emptiness.
